title: Prescribing Fundamentals: Indication, Patient, Drug, Monitoring, Exit Plan
bottomLine: Safe prescribing is a clinical decision process, not a prescription-writing task. Confirm the indication and diagnosis, review patient-specific contraindications and interactions, choose an evidence-supported therapy, define monitoring and duration, counsel clearly, and document what will trigger continuation, adjustment, referral or discontinuation.
recognize: Medication errors often begin before the prescription is written: wrong diagnosis, incomplete medication history, unrecognized pregnancy/renal risk, duplicate therapy or failure to define a treatment goal.
Every new drug can create a prescribing cascade if a new symptom is assumed to be a new disease rather than an adverse effect.
differentiate: A drug being available or commonly used does not make it appropriate for the individual patient.
Starting therapy and renewing therapy are separate decisions; a renewal still requires ongoing indication, benefit and safety review.
assessment: Confirm diagnosis/indication, allergies and prior reactions, all prescribed/OTC/natural products, pregnancy/lactation, renal/hepatic function where relevant, adherence/access, comorbidities, substance use and patient goals.
workup: Obtain only baseline tests needed to establish safety or measure response for the chosen treatment; use current Canadian monographs/guidelines for product-specific requirements.
management: Choose the simplest effective regimen, prescribe with explicit dose/route/frequency/duration instructions, define therapeutic and safety monitoring, and plan follow-up before the patient leaves.
Use non-drug treatment when it offers equal or greater benefit with less harm.
medicationSafety: Avoid therapeutic duplication, unclear PRN indications and interacting high-risk combinations; review renal/hepatic dose suitability and medication reconciliation at transitions.
redFlags: Pregnancy exposure to a high-risk medication
Acute kidney/liver injury affecting drug clearance
No clear indication for a high-risk medication
counselling: Use teach-back for purpose, administration, common adverse effects, serious warning symptoms and what to do if a dose is missed.
followUp: Reassess whether the target outcome improved, whether harms occurred, and whether the medication should continue, change or stop.
examTrap: Choosing the pharmacologically strongest drug before checking whether the patient has a contraindication, interaction or simpler safer option.
oneLinePearl: Every prescription needs an indication, a monitoring plan and an exit plan.
sourceBasis: College of Nurses of Ontario NP and medication practice standards

title: Controlled-Substance Prescribing: Clinical Need Plus Current Legal Authority
bottomLine: Controlled-substance prescribing requires both a defensible clinical indication and current legal/regulatory authority. Verify federal and provincial or territorial requirements, assess overdose and substance-use risk, use the minimum effective exposure, document monitoring and never import U.S. DEA rules into Canadian NP practice.
recognize: Opioids, benzodiazepines, stimulants and other controlled drugs differ in indication, diversion/overdose risk and regulatory requirements.

Canadian controlled-substance rules are changing: the federal Controlled Substances Regulations transition scheduled for October 1, 2026 requires current-source verification before operational decisions.
differentiate: Physical dependence and tolerance are not identical to substance use disorder.
Regulatory compliance does not make a clinically inappropriate prescription safe.
assessment: Confirm indication, prior response, substance-use history, overdose history, mental-health risk, concurrent sedatives/alcohol, respiratory/fall risk, prescription history when available and ability to store medication safely.
workup: Use monitoring such as toxicology, ECG or laboratory testing only when clinically indicated and consistent with the specific treatment plan; verify current jurisdictional documentation/monitoring requirements.
management: Use evidence-based alternatives when appropriate, prescribe the lowest-risk effective regimen, establish refill/monitoring expectations and coordinate one coherent plan when multiple prescribers are involved.
medicationSafety: Opioid plus benzodiazepine/alcohol combinations markedly increase overdose risk; abrupt discontinuation of established opioids or benzodiazepines can cause harm and requires an individualized plan.
redFlags: Lost/stolen medication pattern with safety concern
counselling: Discuss impairment, safe storage/disposal, naloxone where opioid risk warrants it, dependence/withdrawal, and the reason for monitoring without stigmatizing the patient.
followUp: Reassess function/benefit, adverse effects, adherence, aberrant use signals and whether taper, addiction treatment or specialist input is needed.
examTrap: Applying U.S. DEA registration rules to a Canadian NP—or abruptly stopping a long-term controlled medication solely because risk was identified.
oneLinePearl: Controlled prescribing is clinical judgment plus current Canadian authority, not a foreign rulebook.
sourceBasis: Health Canada controlled substances regulatory resources
College of Nurses of Ontario prescribing standards

title: Drug Interactions: Predict Mechanism, Estimate Harm, Change the Plan
bottomLine: An interaction matters when it changes exposure or pharmacodynamic effect enough to alter benefit or harm. Identify mechanism, magnitude, timing and patient vulnerability; then avoid, substitute, separate, dose-adjust or monitor rather than merely documenting that an interaction exists.
recognize: Pharmacokinetic interactions alter absorption, metabolism, transport or elimination; pharmacodynamic interactions add or oppose clinical effects such as bleeding, sedation, QT prolongation, hyperkalemia or hypotension.
A new inhibitor, inducer, renal decline or smoking change can destabilize a previously tolerated regimen.
differentiate: A database alert is not itself a clinical decision; severity and evidence vary.
Food, alcohol, cannabis, tobacco smoke and natural products can participate in clinically important interactions.
assessment: Reconcile all medications/products, timing, organ function and the therapeutic index of affected drugs; identify the clinical consequence that would matter.
workup: Use drug levels, ECG, INR, electrolytes, renal/hepatic testing or symptom monitoring only when appropriate to the interacting agents.
management: Prefer avoiding high-risk combinations when an effective substitute exists; otherwise adjust timing/dose and define a monitoring window based on onset and offset of the interaction.
medicationSafety: High-risk examples include additive CNS depression, anticoagulant/antiplatelet bleeding, QT-prolonging combinations, serotonergic toxicity and interacting narrow-therapeutic-index therapy.
counselling: Tell the patient which OTC/natural products or new prescriptions require a pharmacist/prescriber check and which warning symptoms need urgent care.
followUp: Reassess after adding/removing an interacting drug because both initiation and discontinuation can change exposure.
examTrap: Seeing an interaction alert and stopping an essential drug without assessing severity—or ignoring a serious interaction because both drugs were previously tolerated.
oneLinePearl: Interactions are managed by consequence, mechanism and timing—not by alert count.
sourceBasis: Canadian medication-safety and pharmacy practice resources

title: Adverse Drug Reactions: Is the Drug the Cause and How Dangerous Is It?
bottomLine: When a new symptom appears after medication exposure, assess severity first, then timing, known reaction pattern, dose, interactions, competing diagnoses and response to withdrawal. Do not label every side effect an allergy, and do not rechallenge severe immune or organ reactions casually.
recognize: Adverse reactions include predictable dose-related effects, idiosyncratic reactions, hypersensitivity, organ toxicity, withdrawal and interactions.
Incorrect allergy labels can cause lifelong avoidance of preferred therapy and broader/more toxic alternatives.
differentiate: Intolerance such as isolated nausea is not equivalent to IgE anaphylaxis.
SJS/TEN, DRESS, anaphylaxis, severe organ injury and serious blood dyscrasias are high-risk histories that change future exposure decisions.
assessment: Record exact drug/product, dose, start/stop dates, latency, symptoms, objective findings, treatment required, concomitant drugs and prior tolerance.
workup: Use CBC, renal/hepatic testing, ECG, tryptase, skin/allergy testing or other investigations only when they answer the suspected reaction mechanism/severity.
management: Stop or modify the suspected drug when harm outweighs benefit, provide emergency treatment for severe reactions, document the reaction precisely and refer for allergy assessment/delabelling when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Never casually rechallenge SJS/TEN or another serious immune-mediated reaction; cross-reactivity decisions require drug-class and reaction-specific evidence.
counselling: Explain whether the event is a true allergy, intolerance or uncertain reaction and what future medications require avoidance or specialist review.
followUp: Update every accessible medication/allergy list and complete pharmacovigilance reporting when indicated.
examTrap: Recording 'penicillin allergy' forever after remote isolated GI upset—or re-exposing a patient after a severe cutaneous reaction.
oneLinePearl: Name the reaction, not just the drug.
sourceBasis: Health Canada adverse reaction and MedEffect resources

title: PK/PD for Prescribers: Exposure, Effect, and the Patient in Between
bottomLine: Use pharmacokinetics to predict drug exposure and pharmacodynamics to predict effect. Absorption, distribution, metabolism and elimination interact with receptor sensitivity, disease, age and co-medications; the same dose can therefore produce very different effects in different patients.
recognize: Half-life influences accumulation and time to steady state; clearance changes exposure; volume of distribution affects loading concepts; first-pass metabolism and bioavailability alter route equivalence.
Renal/hepatic disease, pregnancy, frailty and interacting drugs can change both exposure and response.
differentiate: A long half-life does not automatically mean once-daily dosing if pharmacodynamic duration differs.
Serum concentration is useful only when a validated concentration-response/toxicity relationship exists for that drug/clinical question.
assessment: Consider organ function, age/body composition, protein binding, pregnancy, acute illness, route, adherence and interacting inducers/inhibitors.
workup: Use drug levels selectively for narrow-index agents or specific questions such as toxicity, adherence, altered clearance or pregnancy—not as a universal pharmacology test.
management: Adjust dose, interval, route or monitoring based on how the patient changes exposure/effect; allow sufficient time for steady-state response when clinically safe before declaring failure.
medicationSafety: Loading and maintenance doses answer different PK problems; abrupt organ-function change can invalidate a previously safe regimen.
redFlags: Toxicity despite a previously tolerated dose
counselling: Explain why dose changes may follow kidney/liver changes or why a medication effect can persist after stopping.
followUp: Reassess exposure-sensitive medications after meaningful organ-function, interacting-drug or physiologic changes.
examTrap: Changing a chronic medication too rapidly before expected steady-state response—or using a drug level that has no validated clinical target.
oneLinePearl: PK asks what the body does to the drug; PD asks what the drug does to the body.

title: Renal and Hepatic Dose Adjustment: Estimate Clearance, Then Reassess the Clinical State
bottomLine: Dose adjustment is drug-specific and depends on the organ function measure used in the product evidence. Stable CKD and acute kidney injury are not interchangeable; hepatic impairment is even less reducible to one laboratory value. Use the current Canadian monograph and reassess frequently when function is changing.
recognize: Renally cleared drugs can accumulate with reduced filtration/secretion; nephrotoxic drugs can worsen the function used to dose them.
AKI is non-steady-state, so a calculated eGFR may lag behind rapidly changing clearance.
differentiate: eGFR, creatinine clearance and drug-specific renal recommendations are not automatically interchangeable.
High AST/ALT alone does not quantify hepatic drug clearance; synthetic function, portal disease and the drug's metabolism matter.
assessment: Review current/baseline creatinine/eGFR trajectory, urine output when relevant, volume status, dialysis modality, liver disease severity, albumin/INR/bilirubin context and interacting nephro/hepatotoxic drugs.
workup: Use the renal/hepatic measure specified by the monograph/guideline and monitor levels or toxicity when the drug has a validated strategy.
management: Reduce dose, extend interval, choose an alternative or temporarily hold therapy according to drug and clinical urgency; reassess as AKI or hepatic decompensation evolves.
medicationSafety: Do not rely on yesterday's renal function during active AKI; avoid blanket 'renal dosing' without the actual product threshold and indication.
redFlags: High-risk narrow-index drug without reliable monitoring
counselling: Explain why a dose may change temporarily during acute illness and why recovery may require another adjustment.
followUp: Repeat organ-function and medication review after acute changes; restore/retitrate only when clinically appropriate.
examTrap: Using a stable-CKD eGFR dosing table unchanged during rapidly worsening AKI.
oneLinePearl: Dose the drug to the organ function you actually have—not the last stable number.
sourceBasis: Kidney Foundation of Canada and Canadian renal practice resources

title: Antibiotic Selection and Stewardship: Syndrome, Severity, Source, Spectrum, Stop Plan
bottomLine: Antibiotics need a compatible bacterial syndrome and an explicit reassessment plan. Assess severity and source, obtain cultures when they will change care without delaying time-critical therapy, choose the narrowest effective agent using current Canadian/local guidance, then shorten, narrow or stop when evidence permits.
recognize: Positive cultures may represent colonization or contamination; source control may matter more than broader antibiotics.
Recent antibiotics, healthcare exposure, prior resistant organisms, pregnancy, immune status and organ function change empiric choices.
differentiate: Viral respiratory illness, asymptomatic bacteriuria and noninfectious inflammation are common antibiotic-overuse traps.
Sepsis may justify prompt broad empiric therapy initially but still requires de-escalation when data return.
assessment: Define infection syndrome/source, severity/organ dysfunction, allergy history, prior cultures, recent antibiotics, renal/hepatic function, pregnancy and immune status.
workup: Obtain cultures before treatment when indicated and safe; avoid low-value cultures likely to produce colonization-driven overtreatment.
management: Use current national/provincial/local guidance and antibiograms, document dose/route/duration and a culture/clinical review point, and arrange drainage/device removal/other source control when indicated.
medicationSafety: Review allergy validity, C. difficile risk, renal/hepatic dosing, QT/interactions and pregnancy/age considerations.
counselling: When antibiotics are not indicated, validate symptoms and provide an active symptom/return plan rather than a dismissive 'viral' label.
followUp: Review cultures and response; persistent/worsening illness requires diagnostic reassessment, not automatic broadening.
examTrap: Treating a culture result instead of the clinical infection syndrome.
oneLinePearl: Antibiotics require a syndrome, a target and a stop plan.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Using Antibiotics Wisely
Public Health Agency of Canada antimicrobial stewardship resources

title: Anticoagulation Management: Indication, Thrombotic Risk, Bleeding Risk, Renal Function, Plan
bottomLine: Anticoagulants are chosen and monitored by indication, thrombotic risk, bleeding risk, renal/hepatic function, interactions, adherence and procedural context. Warfarin uses INR; DOACs do not use INR to measure routine anticoagulant effect, but they still require clinical and organ-function surveillance.
recognize: AF, VTE and mechanical valves have different evidence and duration decisions.
Renal decline, interacting drugs, frailty/falls, pregnancy and planned procedures can change the safest agent or interruption plan.
differentiate: A normal PT/INR or aPTT does not reliably exclude clinically relevant factor-Xa inhibitor effect.
Bleeding risk informs mitigation and shared decisions but does not automatically outweigh a strong stroke/VTE indication.
assessment: Confirm indication/duration, last dose/adherence, weight, CBC/hemoglobin/platelets, renal/hepatic function, bleeding history, interacting antiplatelets/NSAIDs and upcoming procedures.
workup: Use INR for warfarin; use drug-specific levels/tests only in selected situations where validated/available and management will change.
management: Use a guideline-supported agent/dose for the indication, adjust for organ function and interactions, coordinate peri-procedural interruption/restart and choose reversal based on the actual anticoagulant and severity.
medicationSafety: Avoid duplicate antithrombotic therapy without a clear indication; reassess renal function and bleeding symptoms over time.
redFlags: Urgent surgery with active anticoagulant effect
counselling: Teach bleeding warning signs, adherence, interaction checks and why DOAC doses must not be self-adjusted from INR results.
followUp: Track indication duration, bleeding, thrombotic events, CBC/renal function and procedural plans.
examTrap: Ordering an INR to decide whether a factor-Xa inhibitor is therapeutic.
oneLinePearl: Anticoagulation monitoring follows the drug and indication—not one universal coagulation test.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society atrial fibrillation guidance

title: Pain and Opioid Prescribing: Diagnose the Pain, Restore Function, Reduce Harm
bottomLine: Pain management starts with mechanism, function and goals. Use non-opioid and non-drug therapies when effective; when opioids are appropriate, define a functional target, overdose/interaction risk, follow-up and discontinuation strategy. Do not abruptly taper established therapy or equate persistent pain with opioid indication.
recognize: Nociceptive, neuropathic, nociplastic and cancer/palliative pain have different treatment approaches.
Opioid benefit must be weighed against sedation, constipation, falls, endocrine effects, dependence, overdose and opioid use disorder risk.
differentiate: Tolerance/physical dependence are not OUD; OUD is a behavioural/clinical syndrome.
Acute severe pain, chronic noncancer pain and palliative/end-of-life pain have different goals and risk-benefit frames.
assessment: Assess pain mechanism, function/sleep/mood, prior therapies, substance use/overdose, respiratory disease/OSA, concurrent sedatives, renal/hepatic function and patient goals.
workup: Use imaging/tests only when the pain syndrome/red flags warrant them; monitoring toxicology or prescription history is individualized and should not replace therapeutic alliance.
management: Use multimodal therapy; if opioids are initiated, use the lowest effective exposure with explicit reassessment. Offer naloxone/overdose prevention when risk warrants it and diagnose/treat OUD when present.
medicationSafety: Opioid plus benzodiazepine/alcohol increases overdose risk; methadone/buprenorphine and other specialized therapies require current Canadian scope/guideline awareness.
counselling: Set realistic functional goals, impairment/driving precautions, constipation prevention, storage/disposal and overdose recognition.
followUp: Track function and harms, not pain score alone; taper collaboratively when risks exceed benefit.
examTrap: Escalating an opioid because the pain score remains high despite declining function and increasing sedation.
oneLinePearl: Pain treatment succeeds when function and safety improve—not when a number reaches zero.
sourceBasis: Canadian opioid prescribing and pain-management guidance

title: Diabetes Medication Management: Glycemia, Cardiorenal Benefit, Hypoglycemia, Context
bottomLine: Choose diabetes therapy for the person, not A1C alone. Classification, severity, cardiorenal disease, renal function, hypoglycemia risk, weight goals, pregnancy, frailty, cost/access and preferences all change the safest regimen; metabolic decompensation requires insulin/acute care regardless of chronic A1C strategy.
recognize: Insulin and secretagogues carry greater hypoglycemia risk; SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 receptor agonists can provide cardiorenal benefit in appropriate patients beyond glucose lowering.
Type 1 diabetes requires basal insulin physiology even when oral intake is reduced.
differentiate: A patient at A1C target may still have a cardiorenal indication for a specific therapy.
Older/frail patients with recurrent hypoglycemia may need de-intensification rather than tighter targets.
assessment: Review diabetes type, A1C/glucose/CGM patterns, hypoglycemia, eGFR/albuminuria, CVD/HF, weight, pregnancy, diet/food access, cost/coverage and current regimen.
workup: Monitor A1C/glucose and medication-specific renal/metabolic safety; use ketones/acid-base testing urgently when DKA is possible.
management: Use Diabetes Canada-aligned treatment sequencing, protect basal insulin in type 1 diabetes, and adjust therapy for cardiorenal benefit, hypoglycemia and patient goals.
medicationSafety: SGLT2 inhibitors require sick-day/peri-procedural ketoacidosis precautions; insulin/secretagogues require hypoglycemia prevention; renal function changes drug eligibility/dose.
counselling: Teach hypoglycemia, sick-day rules and why a drug may be chosen for kidney/heart protection even when glucose is acceptable.
followUp: Reassess A1C/glucose patterns, hypoglycemia, weight, organ function, adherence and treatment burden.
examTrap: Delaying insulin during metabolic decompensation because the long-term plan is to add another non-insulin agent.
oneLinePearl: Diabetes drugs treat glucose, organs and risk—not just A1C.
sourceBasis: Diabetes Canada Clinical Practice Guidelines and updates

title: Cardiovascular Medication Management: Indication, Hemodynamics, Organ Function, Outcomes
bottomLine: Cardiovascular drugs are indication-specific. The same beta-blocker, RAAS blocker, diuretic, antithrombotic or lipid drug can be beneficial in one syndrome and harmful in another. Match therapy to diagnosis and outcomes, then monitor BP, perfusion, rhythm, kidney/electrolytes and adverse effects according to the drug.
recognize: HFrEF foundational therapy, hypertension treatment, AF rate control, ischemic secondary prevention and dyslipidemia each have distinct evidence-based medication goals.
Orthostasis, bradycardia, AKI/hyperkalemia and bleeding often reflect treatment interactions rather than disease progression alone.
differentiate: Diuretics improve congestion but are not substitutes for disease-modifying HFrEF therapy.
Rate-slowing drugs can worsen symptomatic bradycardia; ACEi/ARBs are not used during pregnancy.
assessment: Confirm cardiovascular diagnosis/indication, BP/orthostasis, HR/rhythm, volume/perfusion, renal function/electrolytes, pregnancy, bleeding risk and interacting therapies.
workup: Use ECG, renal/electrolytes, lipids, INR or other monitoring only according to the actual drug/indication.
management: Use current Canadian cardiovascular/Hypertension Canada guidance, titrate outcome-improving therapies as tolerated and simplify regimens when adverse effects or frailty outweigh marginal benefit.
medicationSafety: Avoid duplicate RAAS blockade, unreviewed combinations of rate-slowing agents and unnecessary antithrombotic overlap; monitor renal function/potassium after relevant initiation/titration.
redFlags: Pregnancy exposure to contraindicated RAAS therapy
counselling: Explain why medications may be continued for outcome benefit even when symptoms are absent and which symptoms require urgent review.
followUp: Track BP/HR, congestion/perfusion, renal/electrolytes, bleeding and adherence after clinically meaningful changes.
examTrap: Treating all cardiovascular medications as interchangeable 'heart drugs' without checking the syndrome and hemodynamics.
oneLinePearl: Cardiovascular pharmacology starts with the indication and the patient's physiology.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cardiovascular Society guidelines and knowledge-translation pathways

title: Psychiatric Medication Management: Target Diagnosis, Polarity, Safety, Measurement
bottomLine: Psychotropic prescribing starts with the correct syndrome and treatment target. Reassess bipolarity, suicide risk, psychosis, substances and medical contributors before escalating medications; then use class-specific monitoring and a measured treatment trial rather than serial polypharmacy.
recognize: Antidepressants, antipsychotics, mood stabilizers, stimulants and sedatives have different onset, monitoring and withdrawal profiles.
Akathisia, activation, hyponatremia, metabolic disease, movement disorders and medication withdrawal can mimic psychiatric worsening.
differentiate: Antidepressant activation/mania is not simply 'anxiety'.
Antipsychotic polypharmacy and chronic benzodiazepines are not default responses to persistent symptoms.
assessment: Confirm diagnosis/polarity, target symptoms/function, suicide/violence risk, pregnancy, prior response, metabolic/cardiac/renal/hepatic risk, substances and interactions.
workup: Use metabolic, ECG, sodium, CBC, renal/thyroid, drug levels or other monitoring according to agent and patient rather than a generic psych panel.
management: Use CANMAT/CAMH-aligned sequencing, adequate therapeutic trials and psychotherapy/psychosocial treatment; refer when severity, treatment resistance or diagnostic uncertainty exceeds primary-care scope.
medicationSafety: Monitor mania/activation, serotonin syndrome, NMS/EPS, metabolic harm, lithium/valproate toxicity, stimulant cardiovascular/misuse risk and sedative dependence.
counselling: Set expectations for time to benefit, early adverse effects, adherence and discontinuation/taper plans.
followUp: Measure symptoms, function and adverse effects; document why therapy is continued, changed or stopped.
examTrap: Escalating an antidepressant for agitation without checking for emerging bipolar mania or akathisia from another drug.
oneLinePearl: Psychotropic prescribing treats a defined syndrome with a defined monitoring plan.

title: Immunization Management: Current NACI Guidance, Patient Risk, Local Program
bottomLine: Canadian vaccine management is dynamic. Use the current Canadian Immunization Guide and NACI statements plus the patient's provincial or territorial program, age, pregnancy, immune status, medical risk, exposure/travel and prior doses. Do not rely on memorized historical schedules.
recognize: National recommendation, product authorization and provincial public funding are related but not identical.
Immunocompromised patients often need more vaccination planning, while some live vaccines may be contraindicated or timing-sensitive.
differentiate: Minor illness is not usually a contraindication.
A delayed series is generally continued rather than restarted; pregnancy changes which vaccines are indicated or avoided.
assessment: Review reliable vaccine history, age, pregnancy, immune status/therapy, splenic function, chronic disease, travel/occupation, exposure and prior severe reactions.
workup: Use serology only for defined indications; verify current NACI/product/local-program guidance when recommendations have changed.
management: Provide due/catch-up and risk-based vaccines, co-administer when permitted, document correctly and plan future doses; coordinate timing around immunosuppression when needed.
medicationSafety: Screen for true anaphylaxis/component contraindications and live-vaccine contraindications; distinguish expected post-vaccine symptoms from allergy.
redFlags: Suspected vaccine-preventable disease needing public-health action
counselling: Use clear presumptive recommendations, address specific concerns respectfully and explain funding/recommendation differences when relevant.
followUp: Close the loop on outstanding doses, adverse-event reporting and special-risk schedules.
examTrap: Using an outdated pneumococcal/RSV/other schedule from memory instead of checking current Canadian guidance.
oneLinePearl: For vaccines, current NACI guidance beats memory.
sourceBasis: Public Health Agency of Canada Canadian Immunization Guide
National Advisory Committee on Immunization statements
